title: supplyAsync default pool: ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), why use dedicated executor in production
keyPoints: supplyAsync() and runAsync() default to ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), a shared JVM-wide pool with cores - 1 threads.
The common pool is shared by all CompletableFutures, parallel streams, and many frameworks.
Blocking IO on commonPool threads starves everything else in the JVM.
Production rule: always pass a dedicated ExecutorService as the second parameter.
Separate IO pool (many threads, named) from CPU pool (cores threads, named) for proper isolation.
Use bounded queues with rejection policies and named threads for monitoring and debugging.

s1_definition.oneliner: supplyAsync() defaults to ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), a shared JVM-wide pool with only cores - 1 threads; in production, always pass a dedicated executor to avoid blocking IO from starving the entire application.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Default pool** – `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` with parallelism = `Runtime.availableProcessors() - 1` (typically 3 on a 4-core machine).
- **Shared** – the same pool is used by all `CompletableFuture` async methods, `parallelStream()`, `Arrays.parallelSort()`, and many frameworks.
- **Small** – designed for short CPU-bound tasks, not blocking IO.
- **No control** – unnamed threads, no bounded queues, no rejection policies, no monitoring.
- **Fix** – always pass a dedicated `ExecutorService`: `supplyAsync(task, ioPool)` for IO, `supplyAsync(task, cpuPool)` for compute.
- **Named threads** – use custom ThreadFactory for debugging: thread dumps show `io-worker-5` instead of `ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1`.
s1_definition.analogy: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() is like National Bank of India having one shared car for all departments. Delivery, executive travel, and IT errands all share 3 cars. If delivery takes all 3 for long trips, executives cannot travel and the entire bank is stalled. Dedicated executors give each department its own fleet: delivery gets 20 vans, executives get 3 sedans, IT gets 5 bikes.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Default: everything on commonPool (DANGER)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ForkJoinPool.commonPool (3 threads)     │
  │                                          │
  │  supplyAsync()    ──▶ worker-1          │
  │  parallelStream() ──▶ worker-2          │
  │  framework async   ──▶ worker-3          │
  │                                          │
  │  All compete for 3 threads!              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Fix: dedicated pools (SAFE)
  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐
  │  ioPool (50)     │  │  cpuPool (4)     │
  │  io-worker-1..50 │  │  cpu-worker-1..4 │
  │  HTTP, JDBC, IO  │  │  encrypt, sort   │
  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │  commonPool (3)  │  ← free for parallelStream
  └─────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
supplyAsync() defaults to ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), a shared, JVM-wide pool with only cores - 1 threads. In production, this is dangerous because the pool is shared by all CompletableFutures, parallel streams, and many frameworks. Blocking IO on its threads starves everything.

Always pass a dedicated ExecutorService. Separate IO work (many threads, named io-worker-N, bounded queue with CallerRunsPolicy) from CPU work (cores threads, named cpu-worker-N). This leaves commonPool free for parallel streams and framework use. Named threads make thread dumps readable. Bounded queues prevent OOM.

At National Bank of India, payment gateway calls (200ms blocking) ran on commonPool's 3 threads. 100 payments took 7 seconds. Moving to a dedicated 50-thread IO pool cut that to 400ms. The commonPool was freed for reporting parallel streams.

Remember one sentence: never use the default commonPool for blocking IO; always pass a dedicated executor.
